item.title: How to Read Tonic Solfa: A Complete Beginner's Guide
item.dc:creator: Francis
item.description: Learn to read Tonic Solfa: the seven syllables, doh and keys, octave marks, rhythm, la-based minor and chromatic notes, with hymns to practise.
item.content:encoded:
Tonic Solfa is how a great many choirs across Nigeria and West Africa learn new music. A director writes the solfa on a board or sends it on WhatsApp, and within a rehearsal the sopranos, altos, tenors and basses are singing it. If you have ever stood in a choir and felt lost when someone said "start on soh", this guide is for you.

I built NoteFusion so that any song — a recording, a hummed tune, a link — can be written out in Tonic Solfa in seconds. But the solfa is only useful if you can read it, so let's start there. By the end of this guide you will know the seven syllables, how doh moves from key to key, what the commas and apostrophes mean, how rhythm is written, and how minor keys work. Every solfa example below was written by NoteFusion's own solfa engine from the real melody, so you can trust what you see.

What Tonic Solfa is

Tonic Solfa is a way of writing music with syllables instead of notes on a staff. It was developed in England in the nineteenth century, most famously by John Curwen, as a way to teach congregations and schoolchildren to sing from notation. It travelled with churches and mission schools, and it is still how many choirs read music today.

The big idea is that every note is named by its place in the key, not by its fixed pitch. The key note is always doh. The note above it is always ray, and so on up the scale. A tune that goes "doh, me, soh" sounds like the same tune whether you sing it high or low, because the syllables describe the shape of the melody, not the piano keys. This is called movable doh, and it is why solfa is so quick for singers: once you know how the syllables sound against each other, you can sing in any key.

The seven syllables

There are seven notes in a major scale, and each has a syllable. In written solfa we use the first letter of each:

Letter Say it Place in the scale
d doh 1st — the key note, home
r ray 2nd
m me 3rd
f fah 4th
s soh 5th
l lah 6th
t te 7th — leads back up to doh

Here is the scale of G major written the way NoteFusion writes it, with the solfa on top and the letter names underneath:

Sing it slowly from bottom to top. Notice how te wants to rise to doh, and how doh at the top feels like coming home. That feeling of "home" is the key to everything else in this guide.

Doh moves with the key

At the top of every solfa sheet you will see a line like Doh is G. That line is the only place the pitch is fixed: it tells you which note on the piano (or which note your director hums) is doh. Everything else is relative to it.

Here is the opening line of Amazing Grace in G, the key most hymn books use:

And here is exactly the same line moved down a tone to F, which suits lower voices:

The solfa did not change at all. Only the "Doh is" line changed. This is the great strength of solfa for choirs: when your director decides a song is too high for the sopranos, nobody has to learn new notes. You find the new doh and sing what you already know. If you are not sure how to find doh, I have written a separate guide on how to find the doh of any song.

Octave marks: commas and apostrophes

A tune often goes below doh or above the next doh. Solfa shows this with a small mark after the letter:

  • A comma (s,) means the octave below. In Amazing Grace above, the first note is s, — the soh below doh, not the one above it.
  • No mark (s) means the main octave, from doh up to te.
  • An apostrophe (d') means the octave above.

Some older hymn books print these as a small number under or over the letter, or as a short line. They mean the same thing: lower octave or upper octave.

Getting the octave right matters more than it looks. If the sopranos miss the comma and sing s instead of s,, they will start a fifth above doh when the tune actually starts a fourth below it, and the whole line will feel wrong. When you first read a new song, look along the line for commas and apostrophes before you sing.

Reading rhythm

Solfa shows rhythm with the spacing of the notes inside each bar, not with note shapes. In NoteFusion's layout every bar is split into equal cells, and each cell is half a beat:

  • A letter is a new note starting on that half beat.
  • A dash (-) means "keep holding the note before it".
  • An underscore (_) is silence — a rest.
  • The vertical lines are bar lines.

Look at the first line of Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee, which is in 4/4 time, so each bar has four beats and eight cells:

The first bar has four notes, each followed by one dash: four notes of one beat each. In the last bar, the first note is followed by two dashes — it lasts a beat and a half — then a note that lasts only half a beat, then a note held for two beats. Count it out loud, "one-and-two-and-three-and-four-and", moving along one cell for each word, and the rhythm reads itself.

Older printed solfa uses a different style: a colon between beats and a full stop between half beats. It is the same information. Once you can count cells, you can learn that style in a few minutes.

Watch for pickups, too. Amazing Grace starts with a single note before the first full bar — "A-" — so the first bar line comes after it. Many hymns start like this. Count the pickup as the last beat of an imaginary bar and the stress will fall in the right place on "maz".

Minor keys: la-based minor

Some songs sound darker, sadder or more serious. Most of them are in a minor key. The way most choirs in Nigeria and West Africa read a minor key is called la-based minor: the song keeps the doh of its relative major, and its home note becomes lah.

So a song in A minor is written with Doh is C, and it ends on l, rather than d. Here is the A minor scale:

The syllables keep exactly the same meaning they have in major — doh is still doh, me is still me — which means you never have to learn a second set of names for minor keys. Many minor tunes raise the seventh note on the way up to home. In solfa that raised note gets its own name, se (from soh, sharpened):

Sharps and flats inside a key

Sometimes a tune uses a note that is not in its key. Solfa changes the vowel of the syllable to show it:

  • A note raised a semitone takes an e sound: fah becomes fe, soh becomes se, doh becomes de.
  • A note lowered a semitone takes an a sound: te becomes ta, me becomes ma, lah becomes la.

You will meet fe and ta most often in hymns. When you see one, sing it as a step "between" its neighbours, and listen to the piano or your section leader the first few times.

Practise with a real hymn

The best way to learn is with a tune you already know. The Doxology is perfect: every line starts and ends on a long note, and it moves mostly by step. Here are its first two lines:

Try this routine:

  1. Find doh. The sheet says Doh is G. Play G, or have someone hum it, and sing d r m f s up from it.
  2. Find the first note. It is d — doh itself — so you can start straight away.
  3. Sing the solfa slowly, without the words. Say the syllables in rhythm first, then sing them. Notice that the line walks down from d to s, through t, and l, — commas, so below doh.
  4. Add the words. Once the solfa is comfortable, sing the same notes to "Praise God, from whom all blessings flow".
  5. Check yourself. Each hymn page on NoteFusion has a Play button: listen and compare.

When that feels easy, move on to Amazing Grace and Joyful, Joyful, then pick any hymn from the hymns in Tonic Solfa collection.

Mistakes almost every beginner makes

  • Treating doh as C. Doh is wherever the "Doh is" line says it is. If you have learnt fixed do in school, this is the habit to unlearn.
  • Ignoring the octave marks. s, and s are an octave apart. Read the marks before you sing.
  • Rushing the dashes. A dash is part of the note. A note with three dashes after it lasts two full beats, not one.
  • Starting on the wrong beat. Check whether the song has a pickup before the first bar line.
  • Reading minor keys as major. If the sheet says Doh is C but the tune keeps landing on l, it is la-based minor. Let lah be home.

Getting solfa for the songs your choir actually sings

Hymns are a good place to learn, but most choirs also need solfa for new songs: a chorus from a recording, a song from YouTube, a tune someone hums in rehearsal. Writing those out by ear takes time, and it is easy to get a note or an octave wrong.

That is the job NoteFusion does. You can open NoteFusion in your browser, hum a tune, upload a recording or paste a song link, and it writes the melody in movable-doh Tonic Solfa — la-based for minor keys, with octave marks and rhythm laid out exactly like the examples above — together with the staff notation. Then you can play it back, change the key for your choir, and share it.

item.title: How to Find the Doh of Any Song
item.dc:creator: Francis
item.description: Three reliable ways to find the doh of a song: from the key signature, by ear, and by checking the tune. Plus minor keys, starting notes and key changes.
item.content:encoded:
"What's the doh?" is one of the first questions in any rehearsal. Until you know where doh is, the solfa on the board is just letters. Once you know it, everyone can find their first note and the song comes together.

Doh is the key note of a song — its home. This guide gives you three reliable ways to find it: from the key signature on printed music, by ear from a recording, and by checking your answer against the tune. It also covers minor keys, songs that do not start on doh, and how to move doh when a song is too high or too low for your choir.

Tip

If you are new to solfa altogether, start with how to read Tonic Solfa and come back.

What "the doh" means

In movable-doh Tonic Solfa, doh is the first note of the major scale the song is built on. In the key of G, doh is G; in the key of Bb, doh is Bb. Every other syllable is measured from it, so the doh is the one fact you need to turn solfa into real pitches.

For songs in a minor key, most choirs in Nigeria and West Africa read la-based minor. The song keeps the doh of its relative major and treats lah as home. A song in A minor is written with doh on C, and it ends on l. This makes one thing much easier, as you will see next: the key signature alone tells you doh, whether the song is major or minor.

Method 1: read it from the key signature

If you have printed music on a staff, the key signature — the sharps or flats at the start of each line — tells you doh straight away:

  • No sharps or flats: doh is C.
  • Sharps: the last sharp (furthest to the right) is te. Doh is the next note up. One sharp (F♯) means doh is G.
  • Flats: the last flat is fah. With two or more flats, the second-last flat is doh. One flat (B♭) means doh is F.

Here is the whole table:

Key signature Doh Major key Minor key (home note lah)
none C C major A minor
1 sharp G G major E minor
2 sharps D D major B minor
3 sharps A A major F♯ minor
4 sharps E E major C♯ minor
5 sharps B B major G♯ minor
1 flat F F major D minor
2 flats B♭ B♭ major G minor
3 flats E♭ E♭ major C minor
4 flats A♭ A♭ major F minor
5 flats D♭ D♭ major B♭ minor

Because la-based minor uses the relative major's doh, you do not need to decide whether the song is major or minor to find doh from the key signature. You only need that decision to know where the song's home note is: doh for major, lah for minor.

Method 2: find it by ear

Most of the time a choir is not working from printed music. Someone has a recording, or a song from church last Sunday, and you need the doh. Here is a method that works for most songs.

  1. Listen to the very end. Play the last line of the song — or the end of a verse — and hum the final note. Hold it. In most songs this note feels finished, like the music has come home. That is your candidate.
  2. Ask: does it feel bright or dark? If the ending feels settled and bright, the song is probably major and that note is doh. If it feels sad, serious or dark, the song is probably minor and that note is lah.
  3. For a minor song, go up to doh. From lah, doh is three semitones higher — sing l, t, d upwards from your home note and the last one is doh.
  4. Pin it to a pitch. Find the note on a keyboard or a tuner app on your phone, so you can write "Doh is …" at the top of the sheet.

Here is the last line of Amazing Grace. Look at where it ends:

It ends on d. Play a recording of Amazing Grace, hum the last note of "now I see", and you are humming doh.

Be careful with songs that fade out, repeat the chorus endlessly, or end on a held chord in the band. In those, use the end of a verse instead, or the note the melody keeps coming back to.

Method 3: check it against the tune

Whatever method you used, check your answer before you teach the song. Sing d r m f s from your doh, then try the first phrase in solfa. If you have the right doh, the tune will fit the syllables naturally. If you keep needing notes that do not belong — a lot of sharpened or flattened syllables — your doh is probably wrong.

A common trap is assuming that the first note is doh. Very often it is not. Here is the opening of Silent Night:

The doh is Bb, but the song starts on s, — the soh below doh. Amazing Grace does the same. Joyful, Joyful starts on m. So find doh first, then work out the starting note from it, and give your choir the doh and the first note before you begin.

Moving the doh for your choir

Sometimes you know the doh perfectly well, and the song is still uncomfortable: the sopranos strain at the top, or the basses disappear at the bottom. The answer is to move doh. Because solfa is movable, the syllables stay exactly the same — only the "Doh is" line changes.

Here is the opening of Amazing Grace in G:

And the same line with doh moved down to F:

Every syllable is identical. Your choir sings what they already know, just a tone lower. When you choose a new doh, think about the highest and lowest notes of each part, not just the melody: a key that suits the sopranos may push the tenors too high.

When the song changes key

Some songs move to a new key part of the way through — often a final chorus that lifts a step higher. In solfa, doh moves at that point. Hymn books mark the change with a new key at the place it happens, and some show the note that links the two keys with both of its names. When you hear a song lift, find the new home note the same way you found the first one, and mark the change clearly on your sheet so the choir knows where to reset.

Let NoteFusion find the doh for you

Finding doh by ear gets easier with practice, but it is still the step where mistakes creep in, especially with a recording in a key you rarely sing. NoteFusion does it for you: hum a tune, upload a recording or paste a song link and it writes the melody in Tonic Solfa with the doh at the top, spelled the way the key signature spells it. When a melody could reasonably sit in two keys, the app asks you "Which doh is it?" and shows both, so you choose.

And when you need to move the song for your choir, "Transpose for my choir" moves the doh, rewrites the staff, and shows whether each part sits comfortably in the new key.
